newsitem.title: FRANCE: France goes all out ot hit Maastricht target.
newsitem.headline: France goes all out ot hit Maastricht target.

text.p: The French government on Friday cut its growth forceast for 1997 but showed it was still going all out to reduce its public sector deficit in time to qualify for a single European currency.

Finance Minister Jean Arthuis reaffirmed that France would cut its deficit to three percent of gross domestic product next year. "We will reach the target of three percent," he told a news conference.

He revised down his 1997 growth forecast to 2.3 percent from 2.8 percent, though he also said he believed France would still meet its forecast of 1.3 percent growth this year, despite a downturn in the economy in the second quarter.

Despite the slower growth, private economists say they are guardedly optimistic France may near the three percent deficit target next year, a factor reflected in financial markets, which have called off a tentative attack on the franc.
They noted that while the government was seeking to boost consumer confidence by promising 25 billion francs ($4.9 billion) in income tax cuts next year, the net giveaway is actually much smaller.
Seven billion francs are being raised in extra taxes to help fund the welfare system, mostly through higher taxes on savings.
And economists estimate that anything between five and 10 billion francs more will be recouped through higher duties on alcohol, cigarettes and, to a lesser extent, petrol.

Arthuis confirmed on Friday that the increase in petrol duties would be limited to the rise in inflation, but said there would be additional taxes on alcohol and tobacco. Part of the proceeds from this would be used to fund the welfare system.
Government ministers declined to comment on the size of these increases on alcohol and tobacco.
"The exact amount and the methods, honestly, we're not quite there yet," Social Affairs Minister Jacques Barrot said.
But he noted that excise duties on alcohol had not been raised for some time, "so you can imagine that there is some room, and as for tobacco one can also see room there."
Duties on alcohol have not been raised since 1993.
"At the end of the day, people are not going to have a lot more money in their pockets," Smith Barney economist Steve Englander said. "It's not a tax cut, it's a tax shuffle."
The Socialist and Communist opposition and trade unions dismissed the tax reform as a ploy by a conservative government which has already increased taxes by 120 billion francs.
"This is a 25 billion franc exercise in electoral demagogy after having taken 120 billion francs away from households," former Socialist budget minister Henri Emmanuelli said.
The government is looking for new revenue from an unlikely range of sources in its attempt to hit the Maastricht targets.

Government officials confirmed on Friday that 37.5 billion francs to be tranferred from France Telecom next year to the state when it assumes its pension liabilities ahead of partial privatisation would be counted as a state revenue.
But they stressed the money would be held separately from the central government budget and not used to finance either current spending or the tax cuts.
The total public sector deficit includes the central government budget deficit, local authority and welfare spending, and revenues from a range of state-controlled institutions.
"I am willing to believe they can get the deficit down next year to near to three percent through a hotch-potch of highly dubious measures," UBS economist Darren Williams said.
However, economists are waiting to see a detailed breakdown of public finances in the 1997 budget due on September 18.
Next year is the crucial year for deciding which countries are eligible to join the single European currency due to be launched in 1999.
